doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: Playing unknown tunes in Chicago and a Seattle singer in odd keys
summary: Following pianists like Rowles, Hank Jones and Flanagan, growing his ears, then his first US bass job in Seattle with a singer who sang standards in odd keys.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: I always think that the bass player has the most challenging job in the band. I mean I love the bass. And I think it was Marian McPartland who said, via Alec Wilder, “I’d kill for a good bass line.” Something like that. But I’ve often wondered, what do you do, I read about you playing in Chicago with these fellas who would come through. And they call a tune and you don’t know it. And usually the piano player is following the bass player. But if you don’t know it, what do you do in that situation?

Well I mean generally the pianists are the ones that — we hope one of us knows the song. But I learned when the piano players knew it and they would — a really good pianist, particularly coming from that ilk of players, the Jimmy Rowles, the Hank Jones, the Tommy Flanagans, they could lead me, if I could see their hands, they could lead me by watching. I also learned the piano a little bit more because now I started really watching so I knew the names of the notes really well. But then they would just lead me. Sometimes they would go — but eventually it was the harmonic movement that, if I really listened to it — and then I learned — “Do you know this tune?” “No.” “Okay, I’ll play a chorus and then you come in.” The place is packed. And they don’t say what key they’re in, and I can’t see the keyboard. So you end up growing these incredible cauliflower ears, you know, tentacles, or whatever. And I grew them by default. I had to if I was going to survive. And then I had to learn to use the intellect to say, “Oh, it’s in E flat.” And then he goes to something, “Oh, that must be the bridge, well where did that go? Oh, the bridge went to A flat, okay.” So when it came back at least I could start and I

knew where the bridge went, at least I got the door. And then I had to retain that. So that is something that is a skill through repetition, but you have to retain it. And that’s what I think the jazz musicians have sensitized those areas, to retain things that just happen. And how can you somehow develop that. And of course there are different levels of how that comes to you. I mean I could never play some of the things that John Coltrane, that we’ve grown to love, the “Giant Steps” and all that stuff, I mean you can’t give that to someone who just can’t even walk a blues. I mean they just don’t hear, they have no idea. So the diet has to be digested and then expanded. But my rude awakening, because I called myself knowing a lot of tunes, standards and everything, and my very first job, real job, of playing the bass in the United States after I came back from the military, this guy was in Seattle, Washington and it was this guy, he says, “I heard you play at a jam session and I need a bass player. Can you do this gig with me?” He says, “It’s six nights a week and the gig is yours. It’s just me and a singer.” I said yeah. And he said, “We’re just playing standards, you know, ‘All the Things You Are.’” And I said, “Oh I know all those songs, yeah, great.” And I get there and she sings them — she sang them in the wrong keys. And there was no music. And I said, and I thought I knew these songs. Man, talking about scrambling. But eventually, that was a big lesson. That was a huge lesson. And I survived. And I got better at it. And then when I began to hear people talking about, “Well you know you should be able to play in other keys.” And I said, “Yeah.” But it was amazing.
